23:09 Local Time, 10:09 GMT, 15:39 IST: That was some chase! India, Abhishek Sharma in particular, made a mockery of the 199-run target, cruising to victory with 40 balls to spare. It was all about Abhishek, who had a new opening partner in Vaibhav Sooryavanshi today, but that did little to alter his approach. The duo set the tone by smashing Jacob Duffy for 26 runs in the opening over, and there was no looking back from there. Milne, Bracewell, Jamieson - none of them were spared as India raced to 118 in the powerplay, the highest ever in T20Is. Abhishek brought up his fifty off just 15 balls, and although Sooryavanshi departed for a 20-ball 45, the left-hander kept going, reaching his hundred off a mere 35 deliveries. By the time he was dismissed, India had raced to 178 in just 10 overs.

What stood out about Abhishek's knock was his ability to dominate the off side, particularly the cover region, where he scored 51 of his 113 runs. New Zealand tried to replicate India's bowling plan by keeping the ball full and close to yorker length, but India's openers were equal to the task, using their wrists brilliantly and capitalising on the short square boundaries. Mitchell Santner held himself back with two left-handers at the crease and only came on after the opening stand was broken. He did pick up a couple of wickets, but by then, Abhishek had already taken the game well beyond New Zealand's reach. Post-match stuff coming up..

Both teams exchange pleasantries. Santner pauses an extra second to congratulate. Abhishek. Gambhir, Ishan, Vaibhav, Arshdeep and batting coach Sitanshu Kotak cannot hide their smiles. Arshdeep is feeling too cold so he has his hood on. There's a placard that says "Tilak Varma 72 selfie pls?."

Mitch Santner (1/2): [On pretty tough loss] Pretty tough to stop those guys when they're going. We have seen it before, we have seen it in the IPL. Obviously, witnessed it here in New Zealand tonight. [On assessing New Zealand's batting performance and the total they posted at the halfway stage] Yeah, I think I did a little bit early after the ball. It's another lost toss, but, yeah, I think the way that Daryl and BJ kind of got that partnership together, we tracked for 200 there, and obviously 200 is nice. It's a good score on a pitch like that. I thought they bowled really well those last few overs, really got the yorkers in and made it tough for us. So, yeah, reasonably happy. We knew that it was a good wicket. Obviously, when the dew comes in, it's pretty tough to stop, and the powerplay is such a massive part of this game, and they showed, I guess, how to bat in the powerplay.

Why have New Zealand been so indisciplined with the ball? They conceded 17 extras (16 wides and a no-ball) in the first game, 10 (five wides and three no-balls) in the second, and another 13 (10 wides and two no-balls) today in just 13.2 overs. Are India's explosive batters putting the bowlers under pressure and forcing them into errors? Whatever the reason, the Black Caps have looked off-colour, particularly their pacers in the powerplay. They allowed India to race away to 94 in the first game and an astonishing 118 today. The pressure of bowling to an aggressive batting unit is understandable, but New Zealand need to find a way to rein in the extras and strike early. If they are to challenge this formidable Indian batting line-up, greater discipline with the ball and early wickets are imperative.

India have taken an unassailable 3-0 lead in the series, and credit must go to their mental and physical resilience. Having been on the road for a while, they played the first T20I against New Zealand just four days after wrapping up their home series against West Indies. To come here and win the first three games is a testament to their strength and consistency. Can India extend their winning run or will New Zealand finally pull one back? Join us for the fourth T20I on Friday (October 30). Until next time, goodbye and stay safe..
